Five Checks Before You Launch a Loyalty Programme

Loyalty programmes look simple from the outside: customers collect points and the business gains repeat visits. In practice many schemes cost more than they return, because the rewards are generous for people who would have come back anyway and dull for the customers the business actually wants to keep.

Before committing a budget, retailers should check whether they can measure the change a programme is supposed to cause. That means knowing today's repeat-purchase rate for each customer group, the average gap between visits, and how much a typical customer spends in a year. Without that baseline, a programme can run for twelve months and nobody can say whether it worked.

The second check is about the reward itself. A reward that customers can understand in one sentence tends to outperform a complicated tier system, even when the complicated system is worth more on paper.
